title: Dodo Myth Busted: The 'Dumb' Bird Was Smart and Possibly Nocturnal
summary:
For centuries, the dodo has been the poster child for stupidity—a bumbling, flightless bird too dumb to survive. But a new study is flipping that stereotype on its head. Researchers scanned dodo skulls and found no evidence of a small brain. In fact, dodo brains scaled with body size just like their pigeon relatives. So why the 'dumb dodo' myth?

The answer lies in the dodo's optic lobe—the part of the brain that processes visual information. It was extremely reduced, comparable to that of nocturnal birds. 'Our interpretation is that this species was really, really not relying much on sight,' said Sara Citron, the study's first author. 'And the only situation where you're not relying on sight is when there is no light available.' That suggests dodos might have been crepuscular (active at twilight) or even fully nocturnal.

This isn't the first time scientists have defended the dodo's intelligence. A 2024 study found dodos were likely fast and powerful, not slow and clumsy. And a 2016 study concluded they were probably as smart as modern pigeons, which can solve problems and grasp abstract concepts like space and time.

The dumb-dodo myth likely started with sailors' accounts. Dodos had no fear of humans and would run toward the distress calls of other dodos—making them easy to catch. But that behavior wasn't stupidity; it was an evolutionary adaptation to an island with no mammalian predators. They simply never learned to fear us.

Tragically, dodos were wiped out within a century of human arrival on Mauritius in 1598, thanks to hunting and invasive species like rats and pigs. Citron hopes people will stop using 'dodo' as an insult. 'They are intelligent, they are adapted to their environment for millions of years, and the fact that we are destroying it now doesn't mean that they are stupid or they don't deserve to keep living,' she said.

So the next time you hear 'dodo,' think of a clever, night-loving bird—not a fool.
why_it_matters: The dodo myth teaches how easily human misunderstanding can become accepted fact, and how that misunderstanding can hide the real story of an animal's intelligence. It also shows the speed at which human arrival and invasive species can destroy a species that had adapted to a stable island world for millions of years.

background_read: The dodo was a flightless bird that lived only on Mauritius, an island nation in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar; because the island had no native land mammals before humans, the dodo evolved without a fear of predators.
Dutch sailors reached Mauritius in 1598, and within about a century the dodo was extinct, wiped out by hunting and by introduced animals such as rats and pigs that raided nests.
Although the bird disappeared long ago, scientists can study surviving dodo bones and skulls to estimate brain size and infer behavior.
Sara Citron, the first author of the new study, led the analysis of the dodo's reduced optic lobe, which connects the brain to vision and was much smaller than expected for a daytime bird.

Pigeons and doves are close living relatives of the dodo, and because modern pigeons can solve problems and understand abstract concepts like space and time, researchers argue the dodo may have been similarly clever.

perspectives.description: Researchers like Sara Citron see the study as a long-overdue correction to the 'dumb dodo' legend. They argue the bird was intelligent and well adapted to its predator-free island, and that using its name as an insult is unfair.

The old sailor accounts described dodos as foolish because they approached humans without fear. Modern skeptics may still ask whether brain size alone can fully overturn centuries of story, but the study points out that fearlessness was not stupidity.

From an evolutionary view, the dodo's reduced optic lobe and fearlessness make sense for an island with no mammalian predators and perhaps low light activity at dawn or dusk. Its rapid extinction is a textbook case of island species vulnerable to invasive predators and human hunting.

The dodo's fate is a warning for today's island species threatened by invasive predators and habitat loss. The study suggests conservation should focus on the unique adaptations of species, not on reputations, and that protecting them requires systemic action.
